pooled.text: DEPRESSION SCREENING IN COLLEGE STUDENTS 5 The Importance of Screening and Early Identification of Depression in College Students In the United States, more than 33.3% of first-year college students reported symptoms that are consistent with a diagnosable mental health disorder, according to the American Psychological Association (Auerbach et al., 2018). Mental health problems among college students have consistently increased over time and it poses a threat to their health and academic performance (Lipson, Lattie, & Eisenberg, 2019). Identification of mental health disorders among college students have been overlooked. Depression is the second most common mental health disorder among college students in the United States (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students are a key population for determining the economic growth and success of the nation. Thus, primary healthcare providers are the front line to early screening and identification of depression amongst college students. Problem Statement The prevalence of depression has risen in the college population in the past decade. There is an estimation of 33.3% of college students exhibiting significant symptoms of depression, generalized anxiety disorder, or suicide ideation (Oswalt et al., 2018). Depression is one of the most common mental health conditions among college students. In the United States, approximately 26% of individuals ages 18 and older live with a diagnosable mental health disorder in a given year (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students with depression can experience a decrease in physical health, negatively impact mental health, hinder relationships, impede academic endeavors, and decrease quality of life (Pedrelli, Nyer, Yeung, Zulauf, & Wilens, 2015). Research suggests that students who experience average to high levels of well-be- ing also experience better current and long-term outcomes, including academic success, than students who report low levels of well-being. These findings remain true regardless of level of psychological distress and impairment reported by stu- dents. Thus, screening for complete mental health, including both strengths and symptoms may be warranted. Identify students at risk for a mental illness or harm to self or others • Some school teams might screen to identify students who are in the most immediate need of mental health supports. • This can include students who endorse suicidal or homicidal ideation, have a certain number of risk-taking behaviors, or office discipline referrals, and/or experience poor academic progress. • As part of the screening process, screening teams must ensure that referrals to school and community mental health services are provided in a timely manner and that any student who may be a danger to self or others is further assessed immediately to ensure safety. Make economically sound decisions • Early identification of social, emotional, and behavioral difficulties and early intervention services are less costly than long-term, intensive mental health care options such as emergency department care and inpatient hospitalization. • Universal school screening has been shown to connect students and families to cost-effective services such as individual and group outpatient mental health services and support groups.

Available Knowledge/Review of the Literature According to the U.S. Preventative Services Task Force (USPSTF), depression is among the leading causes of disability in individuals 15 years of age and older (Siu & U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF), 2016). By 2020, depressive disorders are predicted to be the second leading cause of disability and death (Soltani, Smith, Beck, & Johnson, 2014). Prevalence of depression among college students accounts for approximately 16.7% and is more than twice as common among college students compared to the general population (Liu et al., 2019; English & Campbell, 2019). Thus, depression is highly prevalent and appears to be increasing. Depression is one of the leading health concerns in college population, yet roughly half of college students with depression receive treatment (English & Campbell, 2019). Mental health among college students affects important outcomes such as social connectedness, academic performance, academic retention, and future economic productivity, which should be a significant concern for certain stakeholders such as campus administrators, college professors, and parents (Lipson, Gaddis, Heinze, & Eisenberg, 2015; Ebert et al., 2018). In addition, depression has been associated with increased health care costs such as emergency department visits and inpatient hospitalizations (Wright et al., 2015). Findings from the National College Health Assessment Loneliness continues to be an important focus for higher education leaders and practitioners, and monitoring loneliness rates provides important context. The National College Health Assessment provides multi-institutional data on college student loneliness. The American College Health Association (ACHA) conducts the NCHA annually and uses the UCLA 3-item loneliness scale to assess student loneliness (Hughes et al., 2004). The scale is comprised of three questions with the responses “hardly ever”, “some of the time” and “often”. These three options are worth 1, 2 and 3 points, respectively. The scores for each question are added together to create a total score from 3 to 9. Those with a score of six or greater are categorized as “lonely.” Loneliness in the National NCHA Sample Recent data from the national sample of university students taking the National College Health Assessment (NCHA) shows that the percentage of students reporting loneliness nationally has significantly decreased between 2022 and 2024. Table 1 shows differences in loneliness over time in the national NCHA sample between 2022 and 2024 (ACHA, 2022; ACHA, 2024). In 2024, approximately 75% of participating institutions were public universities and 94% of institutions were 4-year universities. Mental illnesses such as depression has been associated with significant morbidity, mortality, disability, and increased risk of suicide (Khubchandani, Brey, Kotecki, Kleinfelder, & Anderson, 2016). Efforts to increase awareness and screening of depression among college students should be a priority. Local Problem An identified public college health center had a complaint-based approach to depression screening. A complaint-based approach screens for depression if a patient presented with depression-related symptoms. Patients may mask their depressive symptoms and suicidal intent by complaining of other health issues. Patients may report somatic symptoms in an attempt to avoid mental health stigma. Thus, the complaint-based approach may under-detect and under- treat depression. The Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) could be utilized as a first step approach to screen college students for depression during every visit at the college health center. The PHQ-2 has two questions and can easily be administered by healthcare providers at the college health center. College students who screen positive should be further evaluated with the PHQ-9 and possibly referred to counseling services at the identified public college. The counseling center at the identified public college provides an array of mental health services that could be beneficial for college students who are experiencing depression, but college students should first be screened and identified. Clinical Question In college-aged students (P), how does screening for depression with the Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) (I) compared to current practice (C) affect early identification of depression (O)?
